The essential function is `mizu_channel()`.
It creates a two-way shared-memory channel — one lock-free ring per direction — and spawns a child R process connected to the other end.
The child evaluates a quoted expression with `ch` bound to its side of the channel.
All data crosses the rings, not the process boundary.

``` r
library(mizu)

ch <- mizu_channel(quote(
  repeat {
    x <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
    if (inherits(x, "mizu_sentinel")) break
    mizu_send(ch, x * 2)
  }
))

mizu_send(ch, 21)
mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
#> [1] 42
```

`mizu_send()` publishes a message to the peer, visible the moment the call returns.
`mizu_recv()` returns the next message.
`mizu_send_batch()` and `mizu_recv_batch()` move a whole list of messages in one call.
Use them at rates where the per-call overhead of R itself starts to matter.

Outcomes that end a conversation — ring full, timeout, orderly close, peer death — come back as class-tagged sentinel values, not errors.
A receive loop tests for them with `inherits(x, "mizu_sentinel")`, or with the specific classes `mizu_full`, `mizu_timeout`, `mizu_closed`, `mizu_peer_gone`.
`mizu_is_sentinel()` is the stricter test — identity against the four interned singletons: a class test alone cannot tell a terminal state from a look-alike payload, and a genuine sentinel forwarded as a message arrives as an ordinary copy.
No call needs an error handler.
If the process at the other end dies, receives first drain the messages that it already published, then report `mizu_peer_gone`.
`mizu_alive(ch)` reports at any time whether the peer still runs, without touching the rings.

`mizu_close()` performs an orderly shutdown.
It waits for the peer to finish draining before it releases the shared resources:

``` r
mizu_close(ch)
```

If the code of the peer raises, the error crosses as data: a receive returns a `mizu_error_remote` condition object rather than signalling it.
`mizu_is_remote_error()` tests for one, `conditionMessage()` leads with the remote type, and `mizu_raise()` signals it in your own session:

``` r
ch <- mizu_channel(quote(stop("boom")))
x <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
mizu_is_remote_error(x)
#> [1] TRUE
conditionMessage(x)
#> [1] "simpleError: boom"
mizu_close(ch)
```

The peer also prints an error epilogue to its standard error, which lands on your console by default.
The `launcher` argument customizes the spawn: its default `mizu_launcher()` takes `stdout` / `stderr`, so `launcher = mizu_launcher(stderr = "peer.log")` collects the epilogue in a file instead — the same factory launches the R workers of `mizu_pool()`.

## Promises and handlers

For event-driven consumers — a Shiny app, an `httpuv` server, any program organized around an event loop — the channel arms a notify endpoint instead of parking a thread: a publish signals it at the same already-synchronized checkpoint where a blocking receive is woken, and the signal schedules the resolution on the main thread through `later`.
There is no polling and no extra thread.
Requires the `later` package, and `promises` for the promise forms.

`mizu_recv_async()` returns a promise (never blocks) that resolves with the next message — the identical object a blocking `mizu_recv()` would have returned — and rejects on close, peer death, or its own `timeout`, as classed error conditions carrying the sentinel class names.
`mizu_recv_handler()` is the stream form: it installs a function and each burst is delivered to it from the event loop, with `batch = TRUE` collecting the burst into one list per call.
Resolution is per-burst, never per-item: a promise costs tens of microseconds of R machinery against about a microsecond of transport, so volume belongs on the batch handler, and every main-thread drain is bounded per event-loop quantum and re-scheduled — a saturated ring cannot starve the loop.

``` r
library(promises)
ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_recv_async(ch) %...>% print()
mizu_send(ch, 42L)
for (i in 1:4) later::run_now(1) # pump the loop until the resolution lands
#> [1] 42
mizu_close(ch)
```

A channel holds at most one of the two consumer forms at a time: installing a handler with promises pending, or requesting a promise with a handler installed, is an error.
